strengths: Compelling efficiency results: Fly-CL achieves order-of-magnitude reductions in post-extraction training time (e.g., 91% on CIFAR-100, 83%/67% on CUB/VTAB) with accuracy comparable to or exceeding strong baselines (RanPAC, EASE, F-OAL), demonstrated across ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50 backbones, five datasets, batch and online settings, and longer task sequences.

Thorough and well-organized evaluation: component-wise timing analysis (Table 4), ablation studies (Figure 4), hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Figure 5), memory usage comparisons (Table 8), and domain-shift experiments (Table 6), with 5 random seeds and mean±std reporting.

The system design is sensible and well-motivated: sparse random projection + top-k sparsification for cheap decorrelation, GCV-based adaptive regularization that avoids expensive cross-validation in high dimensions, and Cholesky-based streaming ridge solution form a coherent pipeline with clear complexity accounting.
Reproducibility support is good: pseudocode, detailed experimental setup, hardware/software environment, dataset/model download links, and a code release promise.
The paper is generally well written, with a clear taxonomy of pretrained-model CL methods and useful discussion distinguishing Fly-CL from RanPAC, F-OAL, and RanDumb.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core ingredients are all well-established — random projections and ridge classification in CL already exist in RanPAC and F-OAL, and fly-circuit-inspired sparse hashing dates to Dasgupta et al. (2017). The incremental delta is sparse (rather than dense) projection, top-k sparsification, GCV-based λ selection, and Cholesky factorization — individually classical numerical/algorithmic techniques. The contribution is largely a well-engineered combination rather than a new insight.

The theory is mostly assembled from prior results and is partly misstated: Theorem 4.1 is essentially a corollary of Tao & Vu (2006); Theorem 4.2's bound hinges on Assumption B.2 (energy concentration in few dimensions), which effectively assumes the conclusion rather than proving decorrelation helps. There are inconsistencies: the main text says the error bound 'decays polynomially' with dimension while Appendix B claims 'exponentially'; the examples switch notation from m to d (k = Ω(d^0.5)); and Theorem B.4's proof mislabels the summation index (d vs m).

The multicollinearity motivation is under-supported: the key claim that prototype correlation degrades similarity matching is only illustrated with a small 10-prototype visualization (Figure 3) rather than a systematic analysis, and the connection between the KC→MBON pathway and the streaming ridge classifier is more of an analogical framing than a substantive scientific finding.

Accuracy claims need care: on CIFAR-100 with ViT-B/16, Fly-CL actually trails RanPAC (93.89 vs 94.21); the 'comparable or exceeding SOTA' claim holds mainly in aggregate. Also, RanDumb, discussed at length as a related representation-based method, is not included in the empirical comparisons.

Some implementation choices may raise fairness/robustness questions: dataset-specific normalization strategies appear selected partly on test results (Table 7), and the penalty coefficient range is chosen 'given prior knowledge of high multicollinearity'; hyperparameter defaults (m=10,000, p=300, k=3,000) are tuned on CUB-200-2011.

Wall-clock timing comparisons conflate implementation quality with algorithmic improvement; some absolute speedups (e.g., ridge selection 7.34s → 0.14s) partly reflect avoiding an inefficient baseline implementation rather than a fundamental advance.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: five datasets (CIFAR-100, CUB-200-2011, VTAB, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A), two backbones (ViT-B/16, ResNet-50), multiple runs with standard deviations, plus ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, memory consumption, online CL setting, and longer task sequences.

Strong efficiency results: substantial reductions in post-extraction training time (e.g., 0.21s vs. 67.71s for RanPAC on ImageNet-R) while maintaining accuracy within ~0.3% of SOTA on most benchmarks, which is valuable for the stated real-time/edge deployment motivation.

Well-motivated engineering pipeline with careful system-level optimizations (GCV-based adaptive regularization replacing cross-validation, Cholesky factorization, sparse projection), each quantified separately in Table 4, which strengthens the empirical claim about where the speedup comes from.
The paper is clearly written, with pseudocode, theoretical appendices, detailed experimental setup, and fair treatment of baselines (applying the same normalization strategy to all methods).
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work: the core recipe (random projection + ridge classification on frozen pretrained features for CL) is essentially RanPAC (McDonnell et al., 2023), and streaming analytic classification is F-OAL (Zhuang et al., 2024). The additions (top-k sparsification, GCV λ selection, Cholesky) are incremental optimizations of existing components rather than a fundamentally new method; the 'fly-inspired' framing adds narrative more than technique.

The theoretical contribution is weak and partly circular: Theorem 4.1 is a direct application of Tao & Vu (2006), and the top-k result (Theorem B.4/B.6) relies on Assumption B.2, which essentially assumes the energy-concentration property that makes top-k work—thus the 'bound' largely restates the assumption rather than proving it holds for realistic embeddings. The claimed exponential/polynomial decay statements are inconsistent between the main text (Theorem 4.2) and appendix (Theorem B.6).

The KC→MBON decorrelation story, presented as the paper's central conceptual gap, is superficial: ridge regression with ℓ2 regularization is a classical technique, and the paper provides no biological evidence or rigorous analysis that this mapping genuinely captures a KC→MBON mechanism, weakening contribution 3.

Accuracy is not consistently superior: on CIFAR-100 with ViT-B/16, Fly-CL trails RanPAC (93.89 vs. 94.21), so the headline claim of 'comparable to or exceeding SOTA' is accurate only in the aggregate and on some datasets; the value proposition rests mainly on speed.

Practicality of the m×m streaming Gram matrix (m = 10,000) is questionable for large class counts and further scaling; memory advantages reported in Table 8 depend on the chosen m, and no comparison against simpler alternatives (e.g., RanDumb, or a fixed-λ streaming ridge without GCV) is provided empirically, leaving unclear how much complexity the adaptive regularization actually buys.

Multicollinearity is asserted as the key failure mode of prototype-based CL, but the evidence is limited to correlation heatmaps (Figure 3) on 10 prototypes; no direct link between measured multicollinearity reduction and accuracy gains is established, and the framing borrows heavily from RanPAC's motivation.

strengths: Strong empirical evaluation: experiments span two backbones (ViT-B/16, ResNet-50), five datasets, batch and online CL settings, longer task sequences, and severe domain shift, all with 5 random seeds and mean±std reporting.

Impressive and clearly quantified efficiency gains: Fly-CL achieves 38–93% reductions in post-extraction training time versus the most efficient baselines with comparable or better accuracy (Tables 1–3, 5, 6), plus the lowest memory footprint (Table 8).

Useful component-level analysis (Table 4) that attributes the speedup to specific optimizations (sparse projection, GCV-based λ selection replacing cross-validation, Cholesky factorization), supporting the central efficiency claims rather than only reporting end-to-end numbers.

Thorough ablation and hyperparameter sensitivity studies (Figures 4–5, Table 9) covering projection dimension, weight sparsity, and activation sparsity, with sensible default values and a discussion of the memory-time-accuracy trade-off.

Timely and practically relevant problem: reducing the training-time overhead of representation-based continual learning with pretrained models is important for real-time/edge deployment, and the paper positions its contribution clearly relative to RanPAC, F-OAL, EASE, and prompt-based methods.

Good reproducibility practices: code release promised, implementation details (timm versions, hardware, task splits, λ search ranges) are documented, and baselines are reproduced via the PILOT toolbox with a stated fairness protocol for normalization.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in the core method: the pipeline is essentially RanPAC-style random projection + ridge classification, augmented with known components from the fly-inspired literature — sparse random projection and top-k sparsification (Dasgupta et al., 2017; Ryali et al., 2020) and GCV for ridge parameter selection (Golub et al., 1979). The contribution reads as an efficient engineering recombination rather than a new learning principle, and the closest concurrent work (Zou et al., 2025a) already applies the fly olfactory circuit to CL.

The theoretical analysis is thin and does not substantiate the headline claims. Theorem 4.1 is a direct application of Tao & Vu (2006) to a sparse Gaussian matrix. Theorem 4.2/B.6 assumes precisely what it needs to prove (Assumption B.2 states that the top-k coordinates already concentrate ~all the energy), so the 'performance degradation is bounded' result is nearly tautological and provides no insight into when top-k helps in real pretrained features. Assumption B.3 (Lipschitz downstream loss) is also unstated in terms of an actual classifier.

Internal inconsistency in the theory: the main text (Section 4.1) says the error 'decays polynomially' with dimension, while Appendix B (Theorem B.6 and the surrounding text) claims it 'decays exponentially'; the bullet examples use d (input dimension) rather than m (expanded dimension), and Theorem B.4's proof sums h_i^2 from k+1 to d although h ∈ R^m. These errors suggest the theory was not carefully checked.

The biological motivation is largely a framing device. The claimed gap — 'a clear theory of the KC→MBON contribution to decorrelation' — is addressed by applying standard ridge regression, which does not derive from the circuit structure; the biological plausibility argument is not validated by any analysis of the correspondence beyond narrative analogy.

No method ever beats the strongest baseline on all settings: on CIFAR-100 with ViT-B/16, Fly-CL trails RanPAC by 0.32%. The efficiency-accuracy trade-off story holds, but the paper's claim of 'comparable or exceeding' SOTA leans on efficient baselines rather than the accuracy-optimized ones in some settings.

Potential fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: for ResNet-50, RanPAC's PETL adaptation is removed 'following their original implementation' — this materially changes a primary competitor and deserves more justification; the normalization strategy was tuned for Fly-CL and then imposed on all baselines, which could disadvantage methods calibrated to different preprocessing.

The multicollinearity problem motivating the work is asserted via E[μᵀμ] ≫ 0 and one correlation heatmap (Figure 3, only 10 prototypes, no quantitative metric or error bars); a more rigorous characterization of when decorrelation improves cosine-similarity classification would strengthen the causal story.

Contradiction between metrics: τpost for Fly-CL excludes shared feature-extraction time, but baselines' end-to-end claims mix these two metrics across tables; a consistent efficiency accounting (including the wall-clock impact of the m×m Gram matrix at larger m, which grows quadratically per Table 9) would make the speedup claims more transparent.

strengths: Comprehensive and convincing empirical evaluation: two representative backbones (ViT-B/16, ResNet-50) plus a modern foundation model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), five datasets, longer task sequences, severe domain shift (ImageNet-R/A), an online CL variant, memory analysis, component-level timing breakdown (Table 4), ablations, and hyperparameter sensitivity across multiple settings; results reported over five seeds with standard deviations.

The efficiency contribution is substantial and well-quantified: order-of-magnitude reductions in post-extraction training time (e.g., 0.21s vs 67.71s for RanPAC on ImageNet-R) with accuracy comparable to or better than strong representation-based baselines, addressing a genuine deployment concern (real-time, resource-constrained CL).

The adaptive regularization machinery is technically sound and practically valuable: GCV-based ridge parameter selection avoids O(lm^3) grid search, and the streaming Gram/cross-moment formulation plus Cholesky factorization is a clean, well-analyzed design with complexity analysis provided in pseudocode.

Fair-comparison practices are thoughtful: all baselines use the same data normalization strategy, baseline reproduction via PILOT/official code, and the tau_post metric isolating algorithm-specific compute is a sensible addition.

Good positioning and related work, including a clear discussion distinguishing Fly-CL from Kanerva's SDM, RanPAC, F-OAL, and RanDumb; the paper is generally well written and organized, with ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements included.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: each core ingredient is well established — sparse random projection plus top-k is the classic fly algorithm (Dasgupta et al., 2017), ridge classification on random projections is the core of RanPAC, and streaming analytic/ridge classifiers appear in F-OAL and RanDumb's StreamingLDA. The main new content is efficiency engineering (GCV lambda selection, Cholesky) and pipeline assembly; the biological framing is largely motivational rather than load-bearing.

The theoretical contributions are weak and somewhat overstated: Theorem 4.1 is a direct application of Tao & Vu's random matrix singularity result; Theorem 4.2/B.6 depends on Assumption B.2, which essentially assumes energy concentration (the desired conclusion), with an unspecified constant C. There is also an internal inconsistency: the main text claims the error bound 'decays polynomially' with dimension while Appendix B.6 claims it 'decays exponentially' for the same bound.

Accuracy claims are stronger than the evidence in places: on CIFAR-100 (Table 1) Fly-CL is slightly below RanPAC (93.89 vs 94.21), so 'comparable to or exceeding SOTA' holds only for some settings, and the paper should be more precise about where the accuracy/efficiency trade-off lands.
The Hebbian-rule/ridge-regression equivalence (Section 6) is a standard derivation for linear dynamics and adds limited scientific value despite being presented as a key theoretical contribution.

Evidence for the multicollinearity/decorrelation mechanism is thin: Figure 3 shows Pearson correlations for only 10 randomly selected prototypes, which is anecdotal; a systematic quantification of how decorrelation relates to final accuracy would strengthen the causal story.

Fixed defaults (m=10,000, p=300, k=3,000) and a narrow, prior-knowledge-guided lambda range (10^6-10^9 for ViT) raise mild concerns about generalization of the hyperparameter recipe to new domains, although sensitivity analyses partially mitigate this.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation: five datasets, two (plus one larger) backbones, batch and online settings, longer task sequences, domain-shift datasets, memory usage, and five random seeds with reported deviations — this is more thorough than typical CL submissions.

The efficiency engineering is solid: sparse projection, GCV-based ridge-parameter selection replacing grid-search cross-validation, and Cholesky-based streaming solves yield large, credibly measured speedups (Table 4 decomposes component-level gains).
Comprehensive ablations (Figure 4) and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (Figures 5, 10-13) support the design choices empirically.

Baselines are relevant and recent, including the closest representation-based competitors (RanPAC, F-OAL, EASE), and the paper is generally well written and reproducible (code, pseudocode, environment details).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core method is essentially RanPAC-style random projection + ridge classification, with the projection made sparse (a known fly-algorithm idea, Dasgupta et al. 2017; Liang et al. 2021; Zou et al. 2025b), top-k sparsification, and standard numerical techniques (GCV, Cholesky) swapped in. The 'fly-inspired' framing is narrative packaging rather than a mechanism that is actually validated as biological — no experiment distinguishes Fly-CL from a purely algorithmic sparse-projection variant on biological grounds.

The theoretical contribution is weak and partly self-contradictory. Theorem 4.1 is a direct application of Tao & Vu (2006) to a rescaled sparse matrix. Theorem 4.2 relies on Assumption B.2, which essentially assumes the desired energy concentration with an uncontrolled constant C, so the 'bound' is close to assuming the conclusion. More importantly, the main text (Section 4.2) claims the error bound 'decays polynomially' while Appendix B.6 states the identical bound 'decays exponentially' — the theory has not been carefully checked.

The Section 6 Hebbian/ridge equivalence is a textbook result (expected dynamics of a linear error-correcting rule converge to the least-squares solution, cf. Oja/LMS). Presenting it as a novel bridge between the KC→MBON pathway and ridge classification overstates the contribution; the claimed theoretical novelty about the KC→MBON pathway does not materialize.

The empirical multicollinearity motivation is only illustrated via correlation heatmaps of 10 prototypes (Figure 3); no quantitative analysis links measured prototype correlations to accuracy, so the central problem framing remains anecdotal.

Hyperparameter setup raises fairness and robustness concerns: the ridge candidate range is chosen from 'prior knowledge of high multicollinearity' (10^6–10^9), and m=10,000, p=300, k=3,000 are tuned on CUB-200-2011 and then used everywhere; sensitivity is only spot-checked on a few other settings.

Accuracy is only competitive, not superior, in the main comparisons (e.g., below RanPAC/EASE on CIFAR-100); the paper's contribution therefore rests almost entirely on the efficiency claim, which is an engineering rather than conceptual advance for a top-tier venue.

Minor inconsistencies undermine polish: inference is described with cosine similarity in Section 3 but as an inner product with C in Eq. 7; several citations appear unrelated to the claims they support (e.g., RL references in the limitations section), suggesting padding.

strengths: Strong empirical results: Fly-CL achieves accuracy comparable to or exceeding recent SOTA (RanPAC, EASE, F-OAL) across five datasets, two backbones plus a larger Qwen2.5-VL backbone, with order-of-magnitude reductions in post-extraction training time (e.g., 5.38s vs. 57–583s on CIFAR-100) and lowest memory footprint.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: five random seeds, longer task sequences (Table 5), severe domain shift (Table 6), an online CL variant (Table 3), component-level runtime breakdown mapping theoretical to actual complexity (Table 4), component ablations (Figure 4), and hyperparameter sensitivity across multiple settings.

The streaming ridge formulation with GCV-based adaptive regularization and Cholesky factorization is a genuinely useful engineering contribution, and the paper carefully accounts for where the speedup comes from rather than attributing it vaguely to the bio-inspired design.

Practical relevance is clear: representation-based CIL with near-negligible post-extraction cost (e.g., 0.21s vs. 67.7s for RanPAC on ImageNet-R) addresses a real deployment constraint for edge/real-time CL.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core recipe (sparse random projection + top-k winner-take-all + streaming ridge/analytic learning) closely follows well-established prior work — the fly-inspired algorithm of Dasgupta et al. (2017), StreamingLDA/RanDumb, F-OAL, and RanPAC. The main contribution is a recombination plus systems-level optimization; the 'fly-inspired framing' is largely cosmetic, and the claimed novelty of the KC→MBON decorrelation theory reduces to the classical fact that Hebbian/anti-Hebbian dynamics converge to the ridge solution.

The theory is shallow and partly circular: Theorem 4.2 rests on Assumption B.2 (energy concentration in top dimensions), which essentially assumes what is to be shown; Theorem 4.1's proof is a direct citation of Tao & Vu (2006) without checking the applicability conditions; and the main text (Section 4.1) claims the top-k error bound 'decays polynomially' while Appendix B.6 claims 'exponentially' — an internal inconsistency. None of the theory explains when/why decorrelation of prototypes improves CL accuracy.

On CIFAR-100 (the most standard benchmark), Fly-CL is slightly below the best baseline (93.89 vs. 94.21 for RanPAC), so the accuracy claim is 'comparable' rather than superior; the multicollinearity motivation (Figure 3) is shown on only 10 prototypes and lacks a quantitative link between prototype correlation and accuracy.

RanDumb, the closest related representation-based method, is discussed in Appendix D but absent from the main comparison tables; the rationale for its exclusion should be justified with numbers. Fairness of some baseline configurations (e.g., removing PETL from RanPAC for ResNet-50) also warrants clearer justification.

Presentation issues that should be fixed before acceptance: the code URL in the abstract is empty ('Code is available at .'), typos ('refered', 'imporved', 'aformentioned', 'a Interference-Free'), a duplicated phrase ('downstream tasks for downstream tasks'), and mixed notation (W used for both the projection matrix and its submatrix in Theorem 4.1).
